headlines.title: Bad. Scary. Depressing. Families give blunt one-word description of U.S. economy
headlines.description: Our consumer team collected gobs of revealing data when we asked viewers how they are affording America. And we have lots of telling new statistics from our recent survey, such as: 63% of people said they’re struggling to make ends meet 37% of those viewers can pay their credit card bills each month 25% of respondents told us they owe more than $10,000 on credit cards. One question in our viewer survey didn’t produce any numbers at all. Yet, it stood out the most. “That was my favorite question,” said Lucia Walinchus, Managing Data Editor for NBC- and Telemuno-owned stations. “Because of the answers. There were some very creative things that people put.” We asked viewers to describe today’s economy in one word. Here are some of the most common responses: Horrible Bad Terrible Challenging Unpredictable Disaster Martinez resident Cheyenne Riggs, who holds multiple jobs to make ends meet answered with another one of the more common responses. “Scary,” she said. We asked why she used the word scary. “Because it is scary,” she said. In Oakland, airline worker Sheryl Walton, who says she has drastically cut back her family budget, used a different word to describe the economy. It’s “disheartening,” she said. “Because it’s disappointing to see us in this state.” Gilroy resident Carmen Guzmán sighed before she answered our question about the economy. It’s “depressing,” she said. She explained that she and her husband both work. And yet, the money from two incomes is not enough to get even one step ahead right now. “We’re getting by, I think. I don’t feel we are getting ahead,” she said. “I consider myself part of the middle class. And I do feel the middle class is being left out.” Guzmán says high gas prices have pinched her family the hardest. She’s an educator who commutes 60 miles roundtrip each day from Gilroy to San Jose. Working from home is not an option. “I don’t have that luxury,” she said. “My profession requires me to be in-person in front of students.” Guzmán says she has been spending $120 to $180 a week to gas up. That expense has tanked the family’s budget. The Guzmán family is cutting back to essentials. Case in point: travel. Because flight prices have taken off, far-away vacations are out of the question; thanks to gas prices, even in-state ‘staycations’ are also too expensive. “Now it’s become a ‘daycation’ where it’s just the day somewhere,” Guzmán explained. “Because we can’t afford to rent a hotel.” But Guzmán says she is optimistic. She hopes the results of the midterm election will shift federal policy decisions in favor of family finances and controlling inflation. “It really does limit what we can do and how we can live,” she said. In addition to our local “Affording America” segments on NBC Bay Area, you’ll also see them from time to time on NBC Nightly News with Tom Llamas.

Yet, it stood out the most. “That was my favorite question,” said Lucia Walinchus, Managing Data Editor for NBC- and Telemuno-owned stations. “Because of the answers. There were some very creative things that people put.” We asked viewers to describe today’s economy in one word. Here are some of the most common responses: Horrible Bad Terrible Challenging Unpredictable Disaster Martinez resident Cheyenne Riggs, who holds multiple jobs to make ends meet answered with another one of the more common responses. “Scary,” she said. We asked why she used the word scary. “Because it is scary,” she said. In Oakland, airline worker Sheryl Walton, who says she has drastically cut back her family budget, used a different word to describe the economy. It’s “disheartening,” she said. “Because it’s disappointing to see us in this state.” Gilroy resident Carmen Guzmán sighed before she answered our question about the economy. It’s “depressing,” she said. She explained that she and her husband both work. And yet, the money from two incomes is not enough to get even one step ahead right now. “We’re getting by, I think. I don’t feel we are getting ahead,” she said. “I consider myself part of the middle class. And I do feel the middle class is being left out.” Guzmán says high gas prices have pinched her family the hardest. She’s an educator who commutes 60 miles roundtrip each day from Gilroy to San Jose. Working from home is not an option. “I don’t have that luxury,” she said. “My profession requires me to be in-person in front of students.” Guzmán says she has been spending $120 to $180 a week to gas up. That expense has tanked the family’s budget. The Guzmán family is cutting back to essentials. Case in point: travel. Because flight prices have taken off, far-away vacations are out of the question; thanks to gas prices, even in-state ‘staycations’ are also too expensive. “Now it’s become a ‘daycation’ where it’s just the day somewhere,” Guzmán explained. “Because we can’t afford to rent a hotel.” But Guzmán says she is optimistic. She hopes the results of the midterm election will shift federal policy decisions in favor of family finances and controlling inflation. “It really does limit what we can do and how we can live,” she said.
